# Webhook delivery and verification

A webhook inverts the request direction: instead of a client polling the API, the server posts an event to a URL the client registered. Because that endpoint is exposed to the internet, receivers must verify who sent it. The standard mechanism is a shared signing secret: the sender computes an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw request body and puts the digest in a signature header. The receiver recomputes it over the unmodified bytes — parsing and re-serializing the JSON first changes the bytes and fails verification — and rejects mismatches. Including a timestamp in the signed payload lets receivers also reject old captured deliveries, blunting replay attacks.

Delivery is at-least-once. Networks drop, endpoints time out, and a sender that retries produces duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent: record the event id and ignore it on replay, or make the effect naturally deduplicated. Receivers should acknowledge quickly with a 2xx status and defer real work to a queue; slow responses look like failures and trigger more retries. Senders typically retry with exponential backoff for a bounded period, then mark the delivery failed. Rotate the signing secret by accepting both old and new signatures briefly, and never let a valid-looking signature substitute for checking that the event type and contents actually make sense.
